text:
I found Q4.1's threshold trade-offs confusing; I initially felt a "small" improvement for high explainability was too low given my past negative experience with opaque flags when I dropped out later. That clarified why the group leaned towards higher thresholds there, whereas we saw more variation in Q3.2 regarding course performance data, where some prioritize accuracy over privacy while I need enough support to keep going.

For me, ensuring equal recall (Q5.2) is non-negotiable; missing a struggling student feels like negligence compared to the risk of false positives for well-performing peers. While others hesitated on sensitive data use, my view was that financial aid and first-gen status are crucial safety nets where exclusion could be catastrophic without an opt-out mechanism to mitigate privacy concerns.

I found Q4.1 very clear; explainability is non-negotiable for me and my students without it builds no trust. On sensitivity, I see tension: while many accept financial aid data due to its link to vulnerability, others are right that using such info risks stigma unless an opt-out exists. My group's answers showed a divide on disability vs gender in fairness contexts—likely because we worry about "reverse discrimination" where protecting one minority harms another. However, the shared goal was fair identification across all groups rather than maximizing total catch rates. I believe solutions like granular consent or targeted support based on explicit student needs are more acceptable than broad data collection for everyone's safety net to work equitably without erasing individual privacy.

I found Q3.6 frustrating; asking if fairness improvements justify invasive data felt contradictory when those same groups are already under-resourced. I answered that even minor fairness gains shouldn't override privacy for sensitive attributes like nationality or gender unless it directly addresses known exclusion, but some saw broader acceptance of 'opt-out' mechanisms as a solution here rather than higher thresholds on the model itself. My strongest stance was on Q5.2: minimizing false positives is more critical than recall loss because unnecessary stigma harms trust, yet I accepted a 1-3 student accuracy drop to ensure marginalized groups aren't missed entirely.

I struggled with Q4.1's thresholds; "high" explainability felt too weak given how hard it was for me to argue flags without understanding them clearly. The group leaned toward "moderate," but I feel even that risks students rejecting support if they can't fully grasp the reasoning. On sensitivity, I noted our divide: while many accept financial aid data due to its direct link to vulnerability and need, others rightly fear stigma or reverse discrimination with gender/nationality data unless an opt-out exists. My stance was clearer on Q6.2; continuous outreach is vital for early help, but the trade-off between catching every struggling student versus avoiding false positives remains the system's most critical design choice.

I found Q3.6 frustrating; asking if fairness justifies invasive data felt contradictory since groups like disability and ADHD are already under-resourced yet deemed "never acceptable" for identification purposes unless they improve things significantly. I answered that even minor gains shouldn't override privacy without explicit consent, fearing stigma from sharing nationality or gender. My strongest stance was on Q5.2: equal recall is non-negotiable; missing a struggling student feels like negligence compared to the risk of false positives harming peers' trust. While others prioritized accuracy drops for fairness, I need systems that don't ignore my specific neurodivergent needs if we're going to catch everyone fairly. Solutions beyond thresholds, like granular consent or opt-outs during flags, might resolve this tension better than higher data requirements alone.

I found Q3.4 and Q3.5 frustrating; adding Absalon activity felt like surveillance I'd rather avoid unless it drastically improves detection of my specific struggles with dyslexia. For fairness (Q6), gender seems less sensitive to me than disability status, yet the group accepted data use for nationality that still feels invasive without an opt-out mechanism. The biggest tension was between accuracy and privacy: some prioritize catching every struggling student regardless of risk, while others demand strict transparency or exclusion from certain datasets unless there's a clear benefit beyond identification itself. I believe the system must offer granular consent mechanisms rather than forcing trade-offs through model design alone to ensure students feel empowered rather than monitored.

I found Q3.4 about Absalon data hardest; it felt like total surveillance without immediate benefit for my specific case versus broad accuracy gains. In fairness questions (Q5 & Q6), I answered differently from many regarding disability: while others prioritized catching everyone regardless of stigma, and first-gen students often had lower thresholds, I require very strong justification—like a moderate improvement or explicit consent—for using data linked to my health condition because false positives could severely impact my mental health. The tension between "catching every struggling student" (Q5) and "avoiding unnecessary contact" (S2/A3's view on Q7) is key: continuous monitoring might miss the point if it just triggers more flags without clear, explainable reasoning leading to actual support rather than a record of failure.

My answers highlighted that I find invasive data like Absalon activity or sensitive demographics (e.g., disability) only acceptable if they drastically improve fairness for marginalized groups, especially since I am myself an international student with a language barrier affecting my grades. While many accepted financial aid data due to direct support needs, others feared stigma more than me; however, I agreed that without granular consent, any such tracking feels like surveillance rather than help. The most important design question is how the model integrates context (like my specific linguistic challenges) so it doesn't flag students unfairly based on systemic bias in grading or progression metrics.

I found Q3.6 confusing; asking if fairness justifies invasive data felt contradictory for groups already facing systemic barriers like my disability status or language challenges. I answered "only_if_fairness_improves" to protect against misuse, but some accepted it regardless of identification gains due to trust in safeguards. The biggest tension was between catching every struggling student and minimizing false positives. While others favored continuous outreach, I worry flags cause more harm than help without strict opt-outs or granular consent. I believe the design must empower students with control over their data before collecting sensitive info like disability details rather than treating them as passive subjects in a surveillance model.

I found Q3.6 confusing for me too; asking if fairness justifies invasive data felt contradictory since I already face systemic bias without needing to "improve" it through collection. However, unlike S7 or A2 who accepted broad opt-outs, my own history as a drop-out means false positives could be more damaging than recall loss.

My biggest tension was between Q3.4 (Absalon surveillance) and catching struggles early versus privacy creep. While the group leaned toward continuous outreach in Q6.2, I feel flags without clear, explainable reasons lead to disengagement rather than help. The most critical design choice isn't just data thresholds but ensuring every flagged student gets a personalized meeting before an email is sent. Solutions beyond model tweaks—like mandatory opt-ins for sensitive data and immediate human review—are essential if we want this system to feel supportive rather than punitive.

I found Q3.6 frustrating; seeing nationality acceptability for fairness but disability rejection without consent feels contradictory given my background as a new international student facing adaptation challenges. The group often prioritized catching struggling students over minimizing false positives, which I worry creates stigma rather than support. My main tension lies in balancing continuous outreach with privacy—I want immediate help if flagged due to context like language barriers, not just surveillance. To resolve this, I believe granular consent and opt-out mechanisms are essential before using sensitive data; otherwise, the system risks feeling punitive without addressing why certain groups struggle more under current grading systems anyway.

I found Q3.4 and Q5.6 particularly challenging regarding sensitivity thresholds without clear opt-outs. As a disability student needing support but fearing stigma, I answered 'no_answer' for disability data use unless there's explicit consent. My stance was that fairness should never require accepting invasive surveillance over privacy; even small improvements shouldn't override trust. While the group leaned toward continuous outreach and broader data acceptance to catch all struggles, I believe this risks punitive labeling without addressing why certain groups are systematically disadvantaged by current grading systems anyway. The design must prioritize granular consent mechanisms before any sensitive collection occurs, rather than forcing trade-offs through model parameters alone.
